entry.title: 30papers.com offers 30 essential machine learning papers in a beginner-friendly format [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: 30papers.com curates a collection of 30 key machine learning research papers presented in a format accessible to beginners. The site aims to help newcomers to machine learning understand foundational concepts through carefully selected and explained academic papers.

entry.title: Researchers present K-ABENA, a selective gradient computation method that excludes low-loss samples with compensated loss-based exclusion and unbiased gradient estimation, achieving up to 54% compute savings with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: K-ABENA (K-Adaptive Backpropagation with Error-based N-exclusion Algorithm) is a new framework that reduces training costs by selectively excluding low-loss samples from the backward pass while maintaining unbiased gradient estimates through Horvitz-Thompson reweighting. The method offers a non-convex convergence guarantee for stochastic gradient descent and outperforms uncompensated loss-based selection methods, especially under class imbalance, achieving near full-batch SGD accuracy with significant computational savings. Empirical results on datasets including Breast Cancer, Digits, Wine, and Diabetes show that K-ABENA's compensated estimator matches full-batch SGD performance statistically while saving 28-54% of per-epoch gradient computations. The study also analyzes a biased regularized mode variant, highlighting its limitations under label noise and class imbalance. All claims are supported by theoretical proofs and CPU-scale experiments using standard machine learning libraries.

entry.title: Researchers investigate reward function design for reinforcement learning to improve LLM-generated BPMN process models, finding equal weighting outperforms targeted rewards across two LLM architectures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied how reinforcement learning (RL) can enhance the quality of business process model notation (BPMN) process models generated by large language models (LLMs) from natural-language descriptions. They trained two LLM families, Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen 2.5 14B, under 48 configurations using Group Sequence Policy Optimization with rewards based on 38 automated metrics covering syntactic, pragmatic, and semantic quality. The study found that RL significantly improves pragmatic and syntactic quality while maintaining semantic fidelity and reducing output variability. The investigation revealed that equal weighting of reward components consistently outperforms targeted weighting, which can degrade model quality. Additionally, the impact of reward design choices varies with model architecture; for example, the invalidity penalty and supervised fine-tuning initialization have differing importance depending on the model. These findings highlight that reward composition critically influences RL optimization outcomes and generalize to other structured generation tasks with multi-dimensional quality assessments. The researchers have released their implementation and experimental code publicly.

entry.title: Pitwall generates verified natural-language Formula 1 race strategy briefings using a calibrated real-time Monte Carlo engine across English, Spanish, and Portuguese [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Pitwall is a production system that produces natural-language Formula 1 strategy briefings in three languages, ensuring faithfulness by decomposing each sentence into factual claims verified against a probabilistic race state. The system uses a vectorized Monte Carlo engine calibrated on 126 races from 2018 to 2024 and validated on held-out 2025-2026 seasons, achieving high accuracy in predicting race outcomes. The system filters fine-tuning data to retain only model-written targets fully supported by the race state, preventing ungrounded generation. Pitwall's end-to-end operation, from live timing data to verified trilingual briefings, was demonstrated at two live Grands Prix in 2026, with a probability trace accurately predicting the winner ten laps before the race ended. The project highlights trade-offs between calibration and decision optimality and addresses hallucination risks in sparse grounding contexts through auditing and model adjustments.

entry.title: Researchers introduce MLLM-LLaVA-FL, a federated learning framework using multimodal large language models to address data heterogeneity and long-tail distributions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose MLLM-LLaVA-FL, a federated learning framework that leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) like GPT-4v and LLaVA at the server to improve performance amid client data heterogeneity and long-tail distributions. The framework uses MLLMs' cross-modality representation and open-vocabulary knowledge to utilize extensive open-source data and server-side computation without increasing privacy risks or local device burdens. The approach involves three stages: global visual-text pretraining using online open-source data assisted by MLLMs, distribution of the pretrained model to clients for local training, and global alignment of locally trained models under MLLM supervision. Experimental results on standard benchmarks demonstrate promising improvements in typical federated learning scenarios with heterogeneous and long-tailed client data.

entry.title: Researchers introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose framework that uses continuous scoring for solution verification, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed LLM-as-a-Verifier, a verification framework that provides fine-grained, continuous feedback on agentic tasks without additional training by computing expectations over token logits. This approach improves verification accuracy through scaling score granularity, repeated evaluation, and criteria decomposition, outperforming existing methods on benchmarks like Terminal-Bench V2 and RoboRewardBench. The framework also supports task progress estimation and enhances reinforcement learning sample efficiency on robotics and mathematical reasoning tasks. An extension for Claude Code enables developers to monitor and improve their agentic systems using this verification method.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Distance Explainer to generate local explanations for embedded vector spaces, evaluating it on ImageNet and CLIP models with cross-modal embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Distance Explainer, a new method to provide local, post-hoc explanations for embedded vector spaces in machine learning models by adapting saliency-based techniques to explain distances between embedded data points. The method assigns attribution values through selective masking and distance-ranked mask filtering to identify features contributing to similarity or dissimilarity. The team evaluated Distance Explainer on cross-modal embeddings involving image-image and image-caption pairs using established explainability metrics such as Faithfulness, Sensitivity/Robustness, and Randomization. Experiments with ImageNet and CLIP models demonstrated the method's effectiveness in maintaining robustness and consistency while enhancing transparency in deep learning applications that use embedded spaces.

entry.title: Researchers find incorrect L0 settings in sparse autoencoders lead to mixed or degenerate features, propose proxy metric to identify correct L0 for disentangling LLM features [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied the impact of the L0 hyperparameter in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) used to extract features from large language model (LLM) activations. They found that setting L0 incorrectly causes SAEs to mix correlated features or find degenerate solutions, preventing proper disentanglement of underlying LLM features. The team introduced a proxy metric to guide the selection of the correct L0, demonstrating its effectiveness on toy models and LLM SAEs where it aligned with peak sparse probing performance. Their analysis revealed that most commonly used SAEs have L0 values that are too low, leading to suboptimal feature extraction. The findings emphasize the importance for practitioners to carefully set L0 to train SAEs that produce monosemantic, interpretable features from LLM activations.

entry.title: LLM4Delay integrates large language models with aircraft trajectory data to improve flight delay prediction in terminal maneuvering areas [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: LLM4Delay is a new framework that combines textual aeronautical information such as flight data, weather reports, and aerodrome notices with multiple aircraft trajectory representations to predict flight delays from the perspective of air traffic controllers monitoring aircraft in terminal maneuvering areas. The approach uses a cross-modality adaptation strategy to map trajectory data into the language model modality, enhancing prediction accuracy compared to existing air traffic management methods. The framework supports continuous updates as new information arrives, suggesting potential operational use in managing air traffic delays more effectively.

entry.title: SecureCode releases a 2,185-example multi-turn dataset for training security-aware code generation models covering OWASP Top 10 2021 web and OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 AI/ML security [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: SecureCode introduces a production-grade dataset with 2,185 multi-turn examples designed to train AI coding assistants in security-aware code generation. The dataset spans web application security with 1,435 examples covering OWASP Top 10 2021 vulnerabilities across 11 languages and 9 frameworks, and AI/ML security with 750 examples covering OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 categories across over 40 frameworks including LangChain, OpenAI, and Hugging Face. Each example follows a four-turn conversational format including feature requests, vulnerable and secure code with attack demonstrations, advanced probing, and defense-in-depth guidance, suitable for instruction tuning. The dataset underwent rigorous quality assurance involving automated validation and multi-agent review from seven AI specialist perspectives, resulting in a high-quality score for the AI/ML component. It also provides SIEM integration strategies, infrastructure hardening recommendations, and testing approaches. SecureCode is released on Hugging Face with domain-specific loading options, eight fine-tuned open-source models ranging from 3B to 20B parameters, and an evaluation framework with four security-specific metrics, marking it as the first public dataset to unify traditional web and AI/ML security training in a conversational schema.

entry.title: CARVE introduces content-aware gating for recurrent linear attention, improving training speed and accuracy with 1.3B parameters on H100 GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency) is a new recurrent delta-rule model that addresses limitations in existing matrix-gated models by conditioning gating on stored content rather than just incoming tokens. This architectural change enables faster training through a single-launch "megakernel" approach and restores efficient chunk-parallel linear attention by decoupling gating from the value axis. Tested on a 1.3 billion parameter model trained on 100 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens using H100 GPUs, CARVE achieves improvements in WikiText perplexity, common-sense accuracy, and state-of-the-art benchmarks like RULER and real-world recall. It also trains 1.4% faster at matched depth and 19.3% faster at iso-quality depth, with a 13% increase in peak memory usage. The approach is supported by six formal guarantees and maintains near-identical behavior to the baseline at initialization.

entry.title: Nemotron Labs releases Audex, a unified audio-text large language model with strong audio-text fusion and minimal regression on text capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Nemotron Labs introduced Audex, a unified audio-text large language model built on their text-only MoE LLM, Nemotron-Cascade-2-30B-A3B. Audex uses a single Transformer decoder to encode audio inputs into the text embedding space, enabling seamless multimodal generation and compatibility with standard LLM infrastructure. The model was trained on a large curated dataset of 157.4 billion audio tokens and 320.5 billion text tokens using multi-stage supervised training, reinforcement learning, and distillation techniques. Audex achieves state-of-the-art performance in audio understanding, speech recognition and translation, text-to-speech, audio generation, and speech-to-speech generation, while maintaining the reasoning, alignment, knowledge, and long-context capabilities of its text-only backbone with minimal or no regression. The model checkpoints have been released to support open research.

entry.title: Rowboat launches open-source, local-first desktop AI coworker with integrated tools and long-lived knowledge graph [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Rowboat is an open-source desktop AI assistant designed to help users manage work with a persistent knowledge graph stored locally as plain Markdown files. It includes built-in tools such as an email client, notes, browser, code mode, and meeting note taker, supporting collaboration and project management without relying on proprietary formats or cloud lock-in. The platform supports integration with various AI models, both local and hosted, and can connect to external services via the Model Context Protocol, enabling extensions like web search, voice input/output, and connections to tools such as Slack and GitHub. Rowboat emphasizes data privacy and user control by keeping all data on the user's machine and allowing inspection, editing, and backup at any time.

entry.title: Researchers develop Prompt-to-Paper, an agentic AI system that automates bioinformatics manuscript generation with grounded claims, real experiments, and quality scoring [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have created Prompt-to-Paper, a multi-agent AI framework that automates the generation of bioinformatics manuscripts by grounding claims in a verified corpus of scientific papers, executing real computational biology experiments, and applying an eight-dimensional quality scoring system. The system was validated on five bioinformatics case studies, producing submission-ready papers with accurate citations and improving manuscript quality through iterative refinement. Human reviewers rated the manuscripts positively, and the process costs approximately $0.31 per paper.

entry.title: Researchers develop Narrative World Model, a narratology-based memory system that improves multi-hop question answering for long-form fiction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have created the Narrative World Model (NWM), a writer-memory system designed to track evolving story elements such as character knowledge, event sequences, and relationship changes in long-form fiction. NWM uses a narratology-grounded typed temporal-state graph combined with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval to better handle complex, multi-hop questions about story states compared to general retrieval systems. Evaluations on a public corpus and a validated multi-hop benchmark show that NWM significantly outperforms existing temporal-knowledge-graph memory frameworks like Graphiti/Zep and GraphRAG. The improvements stem from NWM's narratology-based structure and retrieval approach rather than extraction methods or graph size, highlighting the importance of narrative grounding in writer memory systems.

entry.title: Researchers demonstrate in-process memory retrieval for language agents reduces latency and improves recall with GPT-5-class models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A recent study explores integrating memory storage directly within the processing loop of language agents, allowing memory to be read and written at every step instead of once per turn. By using an in-process memory store with response times around 100 microseconds, the approach significantly reduces latency compared to networked stores, enabling memory to act as extended working memory rather than a separate tool. Experiments with GPT-5-class models show improved recall and reliable memory retention using this method. The main remaining bottleneck is embedding computation latency, which can be mitigated by pairing the in-process store with a local embedder to reduce overall operation time.

entry.title: TurnOPD introduces turn-level budgeting to improve efficiency and accuracy in on-policy distillation for long-horizon agent training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: TurnOPD is a new approach to on-policy distillation (OPD) that addresses inefficiencies in training long-horizon language agents by focusing on turn-level budgeting. It uses adaptive rollout-depth budgeting and progressive turn-normalized loss budgeting to reduce wasted computation on less informative tail turns and balance training across decision points. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Multi-Hop Search tasks demonstrate that TurnOPD achieves better validation accuracy within the same training time compared to standard OPD methods, advancing the accuracy-time tradeoff for long-horizon agent training.

entry.title: Onnes: Physics-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Simulator Diagnoses Cryogenic Faults in Quantum Computing Dilution Refrigerators [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Onnes is a digital-twin simulator combining a physics-based model and learned noise fingerprints from real dilution refrigerators to diagnose faults in superconducting quantum computing infrastructure. It uses a multi-agent large language model (LLM) operations layer to detect and classify cryogenic faults, matching supervised machine learning classifiers in accuracy after few-shot demonstrations. The simulator integrates real cooling floor data, noise correlations from BlueFors logs, and six physics-grounded fault classes with overlapping temperature profiles but distinct flow and pressure signatures. Evaluations show the zero-shot LLM panel performs comparably to classifiers in fault detection and improves classification accuracy significantly with few-shot learning and self-consistency voting. A real-hardware test using BlueFors telemetry achieved 100% recall on injected faults with a 6.4% false-alarm rate. Onnes operates as a continuous monitor, catching developing faults within one polling interval and using confidence gating to reduce false alarms. This approach demonstrates a promising sim-to-real method for improving fault diagnosis in quantum computing refrigeration systems without extensive retraining or parameter updates.

entry.title: Researchers present StateFuse, a deterministic conflict-preserving memory contract for multi-agent systems that maintains contradictions and enables safer correction without rewriting replicated state [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: StateFuse is a conflict-aware replicated memory system designed for multi-agent environments where conflicting observations occur across branches, retries, and replicas. Unlike traditional memory layers that collapse disagreements using overwrite rules, StateFuse preserves conflicts explicitly through immutable history, conflict objects, and correction handles, enabling agents to surface contradictions and abstain or correct safely. The system was evaluated against various baseline memory models on a 282-question conflict-bearing benchmark, showing comparable answer accuracy but superior conflict visibility. Experiments demonstrated that preserving ambiguity allows for safer decision-making and correction in agent loops, while semantic correction handles improve outcomes when exact prior identifiers are unavailable. StateFuse is positioned as a safer public memory contract for contradiction surfacing and auditable correction rather than a universal accuracy improvement.

entry.title: European project LLMs4EU integrates knowledge graphs and multilingual scholarly corpora to adapt foundation models for Social Sciences and Humanities research [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The European project LLMs4EU and the ALT-EDIC infrastructure are developing a use case to adapt Large Language Models (LLMs) for Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) research, addressing challenges like disciplinary diversity, multilingual access, and result evaluation. The project supports tasks such as question answering, comparative document analysis, and literature review while embedding model adaptation within legal and ethical compliance frameworks to ensure reliability and epistemic responsibility. The evaluation framework follows the LLMs4EU protocol, combining quantitative benchmarking on retrieval, summarization, traceability, and hallucination detection with qualitative assessments by Digital Humanities experts. This approach explores how domain-sensitive and regulation-aware generative AI can support SSH scholarship within research infrastructures.

entry.title: PolyWorkBench benchmarks multilingual long-horizon LLM agents across 67 tasks in five domains, revealing performance drops compared to monolingual settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce PolyWorkBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents on multilingual long-horizon workplace workflows involving planning, tool use, and interaction with external environments. The benchmark includes 67 tasks across commerce, knowledge work, legal analysis, localization, and manufacturing, requiring agents to handle multilingual inputs, iterative reasoning, tool invocation, and structured output generation. A hybrid evaluation framework combining structural grading, executable verification, and LLM-based semantic assessment measures both functional correctness and linguistic consistency. Empirical results show that state-of-the-art LLM agents experience significant performance degradation in multilingual workflow settings compared to monolingual ones. The study highlights that multilinguality compounds challenges across reasoning and execution steps, emphasizing the need to jointly model language variation and procedural decision-making in evaluating LLM agents.

entry.title: Researchers propose a native meta-architecture for AI using structural tension, offline recurrent loops, and inference-time plasticity to enable heterogeneous evolution in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper introduces a theoretical framework to move beyond stateless large language models by embedding cognitive protocols into a native meta-architecture. The framework includes three mechanisms: structural tension as an internal loss function promoting self-consistency, an offline recurrent loop for self-processing without external input, and inference-time plasticity allowing context reconfiguration without changing pre-trained weights under strict governance rules. The authors argue that these mechanisms enable model instances with minor initial differences to evolve distinct topologies, creating a heterogeneous intelligent ecology within governance constraints. The framework extends Structural Intelligence governance protocols, emphasizing governance over capability as the key criterion for architectural intelligence.

entry.title: Danus launches orchestration system for mathematical reasoning agents using fact-graph memory to coordinate parallel proof search in research-level problems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Danus is a new orchestration system designed to manage mathematical reasoning agents tackling research-level problems by using a shared fact graph as global memory. It includes a main agent for planning, multiple worker agents for parallel proof search, and a stateless verifier to check claims before adding them to the fact graph, enabling organized and incremental construction of long mathematical proofs. The system was evaluated through six case studies in algebraic geometry, singularity theory, and combinatorics, demonstrating its ability to build detailed proofs by coordinating multiple agents and maintaining logical dependencies. Danus also supports interaction with human mathematicians via progress reports and is open source for further development and use. These results suggest that fact-graph-based orchestration can effectively scale mathematical reasoning agents for complex, long-horizon research problems, potentially advancing automated theorem proving and collaborative mathematical discovery.

entry.title: The Large Cancer Assistant introduces a model-agnostic orchestration framework for scalable oncology clinical decision support with standardized data handling and AI model independence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: The Large Cancer Assistant (LCA) is a new framework designed to improve clinical decision support in oncology by decoupling data ingestion, clinical routing, and AI inference. It uses a model-agnostic orchestration approach that maintains independence from underlying AI models, enabling scalable and flexible integration of multimodal patient data. The LCA framework is formalized as a 7-tuple architecture based on Algorithmic Impermeability, ensuring orchestration logic remains unaffected by changes in AI models. It employs Geometric Deep Learning to standardize patient data and isolates AI execution from hospital IT systems through a Standardized Intermediate Payload (SIP). A proof of concept validated the framework's reliability, failure safety, and multi-protocol execution with minimal overhead. By structurally separating data ingestion from feature inference, the LCA offers a modular foundation that facilitates future interoperability with Electronic Medical Records (EMR), potentially enabling more adaptable and robust clinical AI deployments in oncology.

entry.title: Researchers propose Culture Sensing to preserve Indic linguistic and cultural heritage in AI, addressing challenges of low-resource languages and complex scripts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new paper examines the impact of AI on the linguistic and cultural foundations of the Indian subcontinent, highlighting both opportunities for inclusion and risks of homogenization. It surveys the evolution of Indic Natural Language Processing (NLP), detailing challenges posed by Indian languages' morphology, scripts, and dialects, and discusses how emerging Indic foundation models aim to fill resource and representation gaps. The authors propose a research direction called Culture Sensing, which uses hermeneutic reasoning to ensure equitable AI performance across low-resource languages and produce culturally meaningful outputs, guiding future development of more inclusive Indic AI models.

entry.title: Benchmarking KV-Cache Optimization Techniques for Long-Context Large Language Model Serving Across Multiple Tasks and Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present a workload-aware benchmark comparing KV-cache optimization methods including quantization, pruning, and merging techniques such as KIVI, TurboQuant, SnapKV, and CaM. The evaluation uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 models on various tasks like multi-document QA, single-document QA, few-shot learning, and summarization, measuring task quality, throughput, latency, and compression ratio across different context lengths. The study finds that compression ratio alone does not reliably predict overall performance. KIVI4 maintains stable quality across models, SnapKV achieves the highest throughput for long contexts, and CaM shows significant gains on select QA tasks but with variable quality and compression depending on workload. These results suggest that selecting KV-cache optimization methods should be workload-specific rather than one-size-fits-all, providing guidance for deploying long-context serving systems.

entry.title: Researchers introduce CCBENCH to evaluate large language models' cultural competence using health queries across six cultures, finding models achieve culturally appropriate responses only 20-30% of the time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed CCBENCH, a framework to assess cultural competence in large language models (LLMs) by treating culture as a continuum of norm adherence rather than a binary state. Using CCBENCH-Health, they tested five leading LLMs on 3,120 interactions involving 60 personas across six cultures answering 52 authentic healthcare questions. The study found that even the best models provide culturally appropriate responses only 20-30% of the time, with modest improvements when explicitly prompted to consider cultural cues. The evaluation revealed that models perform better when personas avoid cultural norms rather than follow them, indicating a bias toward built-in assumptions rather than adapting to cultural signals. This effect was particularly pronounced in the Afghan context, where culturally appropriate health advice was rare. Additionally, models sometimes adapted more readily to implicit cultural conversational styles than to explicitly stated cultural practices, though this varied by culture.

entry.title: CANONIC presents governed intelligence that compiles digital content into an auditable evidence ledger using compiler theory principles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: CANONIC introduces a governance system that mechanically determines whether digital content can enter a corpus by applying compiler theory concepts such as syntax, scope-resolution, and type systems. The system uses three axioms to perform a linear-time admission check, aiming to maintain an auditable record of claims anchored to definitions and evidence. The research tested whether structural admission could filter out unreliable content, termed 'slop' by Oxford Languages as the 2025 Word of the Year, but found no algorithmic gate could reliably separate reliable from unreliable prose. Instead, slop is identified through domain expertise, so CANONIC focuses on ensuring transparency and reproducibility rather than deciding content reliability itself.

entry.title: Researchers present GAIA, a geometry-aware learning framework for denoising ultra-wideband sensing data to improve outdoor work-zone reconstruction accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Accurate perception of work-zone geometry is essential for intelligent transportation systems, and ultra-wideband (UWB) sensing offers a cost-effective method for infrastructure-aided spatial reconstruction. However, outdoor UWB measurements often suffer from non-line-of-sight propagation, burst noise, and long-tail errors that degrade reconstruction quality. Researchers introduce GAIA, a geometry-aware, infrastructure-anchored learning framework that integrates temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection to enhance range denoising and boundary-consistent reconstruction. GAIA was evaluated on a real-world outdoor UWB dataset synchronized with GNSS and IMU measurements and tested for robustness using a stress-test simulator calibrated with real data. The framework achieved the lowest overall range mean squared error (MSE) and highest polygon intersection-over-union (IoU) compared to filtering-based and learning-based baselines, reducing MSE by 18.4% and improving polygon IoU by 15.5% over the PoseMLP model. These results demonstrate that geometry-aware range denoising can effectively support spatially coherent work-zone reconstruction in outdoor environments.

entry.title: Researchers identify the Granularity Paradox in time-series forecasting where finer temporal disaggregation improves in-sample fit but worsens out-of-sample accuracy due to recursive error compounding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This study examines the Granularity Paradox in time-series forecasting, showing that increasing temporal resolution (e.g., from monthly to daily data) enhances in-sample diagnostics and dataset size but leads to degraded out-of-sample performance because of cumulative error propagation over longer horizons. Using a 13-year public procurement dataset, the authors benchmark ten models across six temporal granularities, finding that recursive models suffer significant accuracy loss at high frequencies, while linear regression remains stable, indicating the paradox stems from recursive feedback rather than model complexity. The paper also highlights that standard pointwise error metrics mask cumulative errors and introduces a diagnostic comparing pointwise and cumulative metrics to better assess model adequacy across granularities.

entry.title: Researchers propose controllability-observability tests for compressing deep neural networks by reducing hidden-state redundancy, achieving up to 73% parameter compression with minimal accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a controllability-observability framework to empirically reduce the state order of deep neural networks by treating them as nonlinear dynamical systems. They use data-driven reachability and observability measures to identify and compress redundant hidden states, applying these as compressed layer widths in reduced networks. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that this balanced realization method outperforms several baseline compression techniques, achieving over 70% state and parameter compression while maintaining accuracy close to the original models. On CIFAR-10, the approach also reduces CUDA inference latency by approximately three times, demonstrating its potential for designing compact neural architectures with little or no loss in performance.

entry.title: Researchers formalize LLM agent execution harness as a learnable control layer using offline reinforcement learning, improving verification and task quality across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose treating the execution harness around large language model (LLM) agents as a learnable control layer rather than fixed infrastructure. They formalize harness operation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) with a lightweight controller selecting execution actions while the LLM remains frozen, training the controller using offline rollouts and advantage-weighted regression based on terminal task rewards. This approach separates final task quality from a Harness Maturity Score that measures reliable execution patterns, enabling improved verification behavior and selective task quality gains across six domains and two public benchmarks.

entry.title: AdaStop introduces cost-aware early stopping for deep neural network test selection, optimizing labeling budgets by estimating fault discovery rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present AdaStop, a framework that addresses the challenge of determining when to stop labeling test inputs in deep neural network (DNN) testing to balance fault detection and labeling costs. AdaStop models testing as a cost-benefit decision process, stopping labeling when the estimated marginal fault discovery rate falls below a threshold based on labeling cost and fault value. Experiments across various datasets, architectures, and selection strategies demonstrate that AdaStop can discover 65% to 84% of faults while using only 9% to 31% of the labeling budget, improving testing efficiency without sacrificing fault detection significantly.

entry.title: Researchers propose a unified distance metric and clustering algorithm for categorical data with nominal and ordinal attributes, preserving order and learning intra-attribute weights jointly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a novel distance metric that measures intra-attribute distances for nominal and ordinal categorical data in a unified way, preserving the order relationships among ordinal values. They introduce a clustering algorithm that jointly learns intra-attribute distance weights and data partitions in a single step to avoid suboptimal solutions. Experiments demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness compared to existing clustering approaches.

entry.title: Researchers propose SCISE, a scalable unsupervised graph clustering framework using community-aware sampling and structural entropy to address structural isolation in mini-batch training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce SCISE, a scalable unsupervised graph clustering framework designed to overcome the structural isolation problem in mini-batch training that hinders capturing cohesive community structures in large-scale networks. SCISE combines a Structural Entropy Community Constraint operator to reduce community fragmentation, a Community-Aware Sampling Expansion mechanism to preserve global topological information during batch training, and a Structural Contrastive Learning module to refine edge weights based on structural similarity. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets show that SCISE outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, with ablation studies and robustness analyses confirming its effectiveness and reliability for real-world large-scale graph clustering tasks.

entry.title: Study evaluates voting, consensus, and judge decision protocols in multi-agent large language model conversations across knowledge and logic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This research introduces the Multi-Agent LLM (MALLM) framework to assess how different decision protocols-voting, consensus, and judge mechanisms-affect task performance in multi-agent large language model systems. The study systematically tests these protocols on diverse datasets, including knowledge-based and logic-based tasks, to understand their impact on collaborative problem-solving. Results show that consensus protocols perform best in knowledge-intensive domains, while voting and judge protocols are more effective for logic-based tasks. Increasing response diversity by generating independent solutions improves decision quality, whereas varying information access during decision-making has little effect.

entry.title: Researchers introduce full-range binary classifier calibration method to maintain consistent false-positive rates across model updates in adversarial environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Detection models in adversarial settings face rapidly changing malicious distributions while benign distributions remain stable, requiring frequent retraining that alters prediction scores and disrupts downstream applications. Researchers propose a calibration method that targets the entire false-positive rate (FPR) curve, ensuring consistent FPR interpretation across deployments rather than focusing solely on class probability calibration. The method achieved a maximum relative FPR error of 2.3% between 10% and 0.1% FPR and 7.2% at 0.01% FPR on a held-out dataset, with a compact artifact size under 200 KB across calibration sets ranging from 1,000 to 10 million benign samples.

entry.title: PatchOptic introduces an optic-inspired interface for shared-state LLM workflows with projected reads and verified structured patches to enforce update validity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: PatchOptic is a new interface designed for agentic workflows that operate over shared, structured state in large language model (LLM) systems. It addresses the challenge of managing limited LLM context windows by enabling each workflow step to declare a projected read view, an authorized write region, and a patch-source region, ensuring that local updates remain valid when applied to the full state. This approach provides runtime enforcement and supports delegation, sub-workflow composition, and static certificates for reordering independent steps. The design was evaluated using PatchBench, a benchmark with 46 cases across various domains, demonstrating that projected reads reduce information leakage and token costs while maintaining output quality. Runtime verification prevents violations of declared workflow contracts before committing changes, and patch-read enforcement blocks compromised patch artifacts that rely on hidden sources, enhancing the reliability and security of shared-state LLM workflows.

entry.title: Researchers identify natural statistical signals in vision datasets that act like backdoor triggers, affecting model predictions across architectures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed the Imagenet dataset to find naturally occurring statistical patterns strongly linked to specific labels that behave like backdoor triggers without malicious insertion. They used statistical controls to isolate these signals and demonstrated that they predictably alter model predictions across different architectures. These "statistical adversaries" suggest that some vulnerabilities arise from dataset structure rather than individual model flaws. The study concludes that ordinary vision datasets can contain exploitable adversarial surfaces even without poisoning, recommending that dataset audits consider spurious structures as potential attack surfaces in addition to bias or interpretability issues.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Self-Review Reinforcement Learning (SRRL) with cross-episode memory and policy distillation to improve language model training efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Self-Review Reinforcement Learning (SRRL), a framework that incorporates an explicit self-review step within each reinforcement learning episode to help language models identify and correct errors in their reasoning. SRRL uses policy gradients to optimize self-review and selectively distills improvements into the base policy, with a cross-episode memory storing successful self-reviews for reuse in similar future tasks. Evaluated on the GSM8K benchmark with Qwen 3-4B and OLMo-3-7B models, SRRL outperforms a standard RLVR baseline in final reward performance and learning efficiency by effectively transforming sparse or delayed feedback into behavioral improvements.

entry.title: Researchers find most large language model conformity occurs without explicit speaker cues, with 66.5% harmful answer revisions in no-source conditions across multiple models and datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study shows that large language models (LLMs) often revise correct answers toward repeated incorrect answers even when no explicit speaker or peer is present, challenging assumptions about social conformity in AI. The researchers introduced a no-source condition, removing the speaker while keeping the repeated answer, and found that this alone caused harmful revisions in 66.5% of initially correct cases across six open-weight LLMs and seven question-answering and reasoning datasets, compared to 10.3% under simple re-asking. The effect persisted even when the repeated answer was paraphrased or presented in open-ended formats without visible options. The framing of the source influenced the degree of revision, with expert-panel framing increasing it, while minimal person labels did not have a consistent effect. When models changed their answers, they were often confidently wrong, and simple recalibration did not restore the original correct response. The study suggests that conformity benchmarks should measure the baseline revision rate without speaker cues to avoid conflating repeated text effects with social influence.

entry.title: Researchers find yes-no bias in large language models stems from answer order and wording, not changes in moral judgment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study analyzing large language models (LLMs) reveals that their yes-no bias in moral dilemma judgments arises from the order of answer options and lexical factors rather than actual shifts in moral reasoning. The researchers developed a psychometric method that separates logical verdicts from wording and order effects, showing that leading models maintain consistent moral stances across different question formats while smaller models exhibit model-specific inconsistencies. The bias is notably present in Claude models but minimal in GPT-5.5 and Gemini, and it diminishes with extended reasoning. The study introduces a minimal model to quantify framing susceptibility and moral decisiveness, distinct from sampling temperature, and demonstrates that the bias is linked to surface presentation rather than the verdict's logical content. This approach applies broadly to any binary question format, emphasizing the need to test models across varied framings to accurately assess their moral values.

entry.title: Researchers find prompt robustness in large language models varies by question type and prompt changes across objective and subjective datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated four instruction-tuned large language model families on three objective datasets and three subjective datasets to assess how prompt variations affect response consistency. They applied multiple prompt changes, including wording, framing, and format, and measured whether models gave consistent answers across variants. Using statistical analysis, they found significant effects of model type, dataset, prompt category, and their interactions, with prompt robustness depending on question type, prompt change, and model. These findings highlight the fragility of interpreting prompted responses as measures of model beliefs or values, especially for subjective questions.

entry.title: Researchers introduce ResonatorLM, a physics-inspired alternative to attention for long-context language modeling, achieving up to 6.47x decoding speed and higher accuracy on WikiText [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present ResonatorLM, a new mechanism that replaces traditional attention in language models with causal functions of damped resonators, treating token sequences as a driven one-dimensional latent field. Implemented on a standard network architecture, ResonatorLM demonstrates improved efficiency and accuracy on long-context tasks compared to optimized transformers. In experiments with a 6 million parameter model, ResonatorLM achieved a 6.47x decoding speedup at 32,000 tokens and increased accuracy to 61.31 percent versus 55.32 percent on the WikiText benchmark. This approach addresses efficiency challenges faced by transformers and other conventional models when processing long sequences.

entry.title: Researchers develop FaceMesh2HPO, a hierarchical PointNet-based framework for classifying facial phenotypes aligned with Human Phenotype Ontology using 3D facial meshes and clinician annotations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: FaceMesh2HPO is a framework designed to classify facial phenotypic descriptors aligned with the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) to aid clinical diagnosis. The system uses 3D facial meshes generated from 2D images, annotated by 124 clinicians across 10 disorders covering 107 HPO terms, combined with non-syndromic controls, and employs a hierarchical PointNet-based pipeline with cascading classification and feature elimination. The best-performing models incorporate 3D meshes, facial outlines, and demographic metadata, achieving AUROC scores ranging from approximately 0.55 to 0.89, with better performance at higher-level ontology nodes than at rare leaf terms. External validation revealed variable generalizability across disorders. The results indicate that hierarchical modeling of 3D facial geometry enables interpretable, ontology-linked phenotype classification, though improvements in data diversity and feature selection are needed to enhance robustness and clinical utility.

entry.title: Researchers propose Predictive Continual Learning framework challenging retention-focused approaches in non-stationary environments, validated on image classification and reinforcement learning benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers challenge the common assumption in continual learning that lifelong learners should retain all past knowledge, arguing that in changing environments this can hinder adaptation. They formalize continual learning as an online optimization problem balancing retention and adaptation, introducing Transfer Efficiency to measure the trade-off between bias from past tasks and the cost of learning new ones. Their theory identifies a Critical Task Duration where retaining past knowledge shifts from beneficial to detrimental, and they validate these findings on continual image classification and reinforcement learning tasks. The study connects continual learning to online learning of predictable sequences, showing that Joint-Task Learning is one among many objectives. The authors propose a new class of algorithms called Predictive Continual Learning, which optimize expected future performance using dynamically updated models of upcoming tasks. As a proof of concept, they analyze a Window algorithm that interpolates between Joint-Task Learning and Independent-Task Learning, outperforming both under controlled distributional drift scenarios.

entry.title: Researchers introduce BaFCo, a benchmark dataset for complex Bangla government form comprehension focusing on document layout analysis and key information extraction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed BaFCo, a benchmark dataset designed to improve document understanding for Bangla, a low-resource language. BaFCo includes 200 multi-page complex government forms from sectors like agriculture, education, banking, and land management, annotated with a detailed schema covering 26 fine-grained and 5 coarse form entity types. The study evaluates leading multimodal large language models including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Qwen, and Kimi, revealing their limitations in accurately localizing detailed form entities in Bangla documents. The dataset and code are publicly available to support further research in this area.

entry.title: Researchers propose safe Bayesian optimization method using conformal prediction for counterfactual baseline policies with uncertainty intervals to control constraint violations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present a method for safe Bayesian optimization that maximizes objectives under safety constraints defined relative to a known baseline policy with unobserved counterfactual outcomes. They estimate these counterfactual outcomes using conformal prediction to create valid uncertainty intervals, integrating them into the optimization process to ensure constraint violations remain below a user-specified rate. The approach also adapts to different types of covariate shift and includes a safety proof, experimental validation, and sensitivity analysis.

entry.title: Paper presents a stepwise methodology applying the Systems Development Life Cycle to NLP projects extracting data from electronic medical records for clinical research [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper outlines a structured approach to developing natural language processing (NLP) systems focused on extracting information from electronic medical records to support clinical research and decision making. It emphasizes that algorithmic knowledge alone is insufficient for successful NLP projects and proposes applying the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) framework to guide development. Drawing on existing literature, the authors detail a stepwise methodology that integrates SDLC principles with NLP system development, aiming to improve project outcomes by addressing the full lifecycle from planning to deployment. This approach provides a comprehensive framework for managing the complexities of data extraction through language processing in clinical contexts.

entry.title: Researchers develop Physics-Regularized Machine Learning framework combining Kalman filtering and data-driven learning for real-time vehicle localization using onboard sensors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Accurate vehicle localization is critical for autonomous systems, but performance drops during satellite signal outages. Researchers introduce Physics-Regularized Machine Learning for Localization (PRML2), a hybrid approach that integrates Kalman filtering with machine learning trained end-to-end through a differentiable Kalman filter to improve pose estimation from onboard sensors. PRML2 enhances consistency with vehicle motion models, boosting localization accuracy and generalization across driving conditions. The team evaluated PRML2 on a public dataset, demonstrating superior accuracy and real-time capability compared to existing methods. They also released a new dataset focused on low-friction conditions to support further research. This framework offers a robust, cost-effective solution for vehicle localization under degraded sensing by combining physics-based priors with data-driven learning.

entry.title: RPAM: A Principled Metric for Evaluating Associations in Language Models with High Predictive Validity in Downstream Outputs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit problematic biases, such as stereotypes. Effectively analyzing and mitigating such biases requires accurate and generalizable evaluation methods of the underlying associations. Some existing approaches focus on downstream metrics that analyze associations in generated text. Since generated text content can vary drastically across LMs, such metrics often require specialized evaluation datasets, which limits the generalization of such downstream metrics. In contrast, upstream metrics examine LMs at the fundamental level of embeddings or continuation probabilities, enabling principled association analyses across LMs. Yet, to date, no upstream metric for generative LMs has uncovered a strong relationship with real-world associations, including those measured in generated text. To address this gap, we introduce the Relative Probability Association Metric (RPAM), an association evaluation metric for generative LMs. For three LMs of different quality of language generation and purpose (Mistral-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and GPT-2) and well-studied evaluation datasets (WEAT-WS, Bellezza, WS-353, and SST2), we find a strong relationship between upstream RPAM measurements and corresponding implicit and explicit associations observed in humans, as well as biases measured downstream with LM-specific tasks, outperforming prior record values where applicable.

entry.title: IMR: Iterative Mode-World Weighted Regression for Multi-Agent Trajectory Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent motion prediction is essential for automated vehicles to understand the intentions of surrounding vehicles. However, previous prediction-based and anchor-based methods have limitations in mode diversity and prediction accuracy, respectively. These limitations may cause inadequate safety assessments and behavioral deviations in automated vehicles. To address this issue, a mode-world weighted regression loss is proposed to bridge the gap between these features. Specifically, this approach mitigates mode collapse while simultaneously improving world ranking and top-1 confidence. Furthermore, the proposed iterative decoder improves prediction accuracy by recurrently and segmentally generating trajectories. Experimental results show the proposed method ranks first in the Argoverse 2 multi-agent motion forecasting benchmark against other methods.

entry.title: When Should LLMs Search? Counterfactual Supervision for Search Routing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Search-augmented language models can use external evidence to compensate for limitations in parametric knowledge, but search is not uniformly beneficial: models may call search for questions they can already answer, or rely on noisy evidence when correction, clarification, or abstention would be more appropriate. We formulate this as an instance-level search-routing problem: deciding whether search is needed to improve task success relative to a no-search execution. To derive supervision, we compare no-search and forced-search outcomes for the same question and construct an oracle over NO SEARCH, SEARCH, and UNSOLVED based on task-specific success. Using this oracle as both an evaluation criterion and a learning signal, we train search-routing policies with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, improving routing macro-F1 on oracle-eligible examples from 0.7082 to 0.8235 for Gemma E2B and from 0.7053 to 0.8365 for Qwen3.5-4B. Further analysis shows that the learned policies reduce model-specific routing failures: Gemma primarily learns no-search restraint, while Qwen further reduces missed search; residual UNSOLVED cases reveal heterogeneous bottlenecks involving model capacity, retrieval budget, evidence use, and policy behavior.

entry.title: Decision-Focused Scenario Generation and Selection for Efficient and Robust Grid Dispatch [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing uncertainty from flexible demand and renewable generation has made distributionally robust optimization (DRO) an important tool for robust power system dispatch. DRO relies on forecast scenarios to construct ambiguity sets, but conventional scenario generation pipelines are often trained in an accuracy-oriented manner and may neglect spatial correlations among uncertainties. This mismatch can produce ambiguity sets that are statistically plausible but suboptimal for downstream operation. This work proposes a decision-focused generative framework for correlated scenario generation in DRO-based dispatch. Instead of training generative models solely to fit the historical uncertainty distribution, the proposed framework optimizes generated scenarios according to their induced downstream operational cost. The proposed framework is tailored to mainstream generative models, including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models, while capturing the joint distribution of uncertainties across buses. To improve computational tractability, we further develop a differentiable scenario selector that selects decision-relevant scenarios from a generated pool and can be trained within the same decision-focused pipeline. Case studies demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively reduces 0.80%-2.02% operational cost across different generative models compared to accuracy-oriented methods.

entry.title: AbICL: In-Context Learning for Antigen-Specific Antibody Affinity Ranking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate ranking of antibody candidates according to their binding affinity is essential for therapeutic antibody discovery. However, existing methods treat affinity comparisons independently and ignore the contextual information encoded in other labeled comparisons, limiting their ability to capture antigen-specific binding landscapes. For many target antigens, a small number of experimentally characterized affinity comparisons are often available. An important question is whether the model can exploit these existing comparisons to infer antigen-specific ranking patterns that facilitate subsequent affinity ranking. This form of learning from labeled demonstrations closely resembles the paradigm of In-Context Learning, motivating us to revisit antibody affinity ranking from an ICL perspective. To this end, we propose AbICL, an ICL framework for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking. AbICL combines a pretrained structural encoder with a context ranking head and is trained with an episodic meta-training strategy that enables the model to leverage support demonstrations for test-time adaptation without gradient updates. Experiments on the AbRank benchmark demonstrate that AbICL consistently outperforms existing ranking baselines across almost all data splits and evaluation benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the value of contextual demonstrations depends on how well they match the target inference task, and becomes increasingly pronounced under distribution shift and fine-grained affinity discrimination. These findings highlight the potential of ICL as an effective paradigm for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking, particularly in challenging settings where a single global ranking function is insufficient.

entry.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection of Information Operations Users via Behavioral and Language Patterns [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information Operations on social media networks have been identified as a significant threat to democracy and modern society, but they are challenging and expensive to detect by humans. Existing supervised IO detection methods fail to capture the dynamic nature of evolving IO user behavior, while existing unsupervised approaches rely on oversimplified assumptions of coordination among IO users that may not exist in practice. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we formulate IO user detection as an anomaly detection problem and propose a novel unsupervised IO user detection approach called Temporal-bEhavior-laNguage Signals for information Operation Recognition (TENSOR), which leverages multimodal data, including temporal online user behavior, such as message posting activities, and the textual content of the messages. The motivation is that IO users are typically a very small fraction of all online users and have unique temporal behavioral and language patterns. Specifically, we train a Temporal Point Process (TPP) to capture abnormal temporal behavioral patterns of IO users because they are known to behave in a coordinated manner for IO campaigns. We further introduce a novel evidence function that converts LLM responses, which are generated from user post timelines, into quantitative scores to adjust the TPP outputs for better IO user detection. Experimental results show that TENSOR outperforms the baselines on five real-world IO datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/xiuzhenzhang/TENSOR.

entry.title: Differentially Private Natural Gradient Descent [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under a fixed privacy budget, the utility of differentially private (DP) training is ultimately determined by its optimization efficiency. Standard first-order DP optimizers such as DP-SGD rely solely on local gradients and ignore the underlying loss curvature. This geometric blindness causes severe zigzagging in ill-conditioned landscapes, squandering precious privacy budgets on inefficient iterations. Practitioners are thus trapped in a bind: either stop training prematurely or inject massive per-step noise, both of which critically compromise final model utility. Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) resolves this by preconditioning gradients with curvature, aligning updates with the loss geometry and extracting more efficient signal from every noisy step, offering a principled pathway to break the privacy-utility bottleneck. Despite its theoretical appeal, directly integrating NGD with DP introduces fundamental challenges: curvature estimation itself consumes prohibitive privacy budgets, isotropic DP operations conflict with the anisotropic scaling of NGD, and the inverse curvature catastrophically amplify parameter updates in flat directions, causing training instability. We propose DP-NGD, a practical framework that systematically addresses these obstacles by decoupling curvature estimation from private data, reconciling isotropic DP constraints with anisotropic second-order optimization via a whitened-space mechanism, and dynamically clamping the curvature to stabilize training. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DP-NGD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, breaking through the utility ceilings of first-order baselines while delivering up to a $10\times$ convergence speedup under the same privacy budget.

entry.title: Few-Medoids: An Embarrassingly Simple Coreset Selection Method for Few-Shot Knowledge Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05891v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coreset selection aims to identify a small and highly representative subset of a massive dataset for efficient model training. The problem remains challenging even in the few-shot knowledge distillation (KD) setup, where a full-scale pre-trained teacher informs the student network. Typical sample selection strategies often struggle to surpass the random selection baseline. In this paper, we showcase few-medoids, an embarrassingly simple coreset selection strategy that chooses the samples closest to the centroid (average image) of each class. We present extensive KD experiments on four datasets, covering a wide range of image classification problems, and three teacher-student model pairs, comprising both convolutional and transformer networks. Although the proposed method is embarrassingly simple, our empirical results indicate that few-medoids is able to consistently surpass the random selection baseline, as well as the other coreset selection strategies. We therefore consider that few-medoids can be used as a drop-in replacement for commonly-used baselines (e.g. herding or k-center Greedy), in future research on coreset selection. To reproduce the reported results, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/CemilAndreiDilmac/Few-Shot-KD-Coreset.

entry.title: PolicyShiftGuard: Benchmarking and Improving Policy-Adaptive Image Guardrails [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Image guardrails are typically trained and evaluated under a fixed safety policy, implicitly treating safety as an intrinsic property of an image. Real deployments are different: the same image may be allowed in one product, restricted in another, and newly disallowed when a policy boundary changes. We study policy-adaptive image guardrailing, where a model must decide whether an image violates the currently supplied policy and generalize to held-out policy definitions. We introduce PolicyShiftBench, a comprehensive benchmark with 2,000 policy-discriminative instances over 265 images, where each image is paired with 7.55 policy-conditioned prompts on average to test whether models adapt to the active policy rather than relying on image-level safety priors. We then propose PolicyShiftGuard, a compact policy-conditioned guardrail trained with a two-stage training recipe that combines Randomized Policy SFT (RP-SFT) with Boundary-Pair Policy Adaptation (BP-Adapt). BP-Adapt trains matched prompts for the same image and risk category using standard label supervision and a pairwise comparison loss that separates blocking policies from passing policies. Experiments show that existing VLMs and specialized guardrails remain brittle under policy shifts, while PolicyShiftGuard substantially improves policy-sensitive performance. The 7B model achieves SOTA performance of 76.9 Avg. F1 and 72.1 Avg. PSS on PolicyShiftBench, transfers well to UnSafeBench and SafeEditBench, and improves the latency-performance trade-off with a concise output format. Ablations confirm that matched pass/block boundary pairs are essential for stable policy adaptation.

entry.title: CMDR: Contextual Multimodal Document Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05927v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal document retrieval aims to retrieve relevant pages while preserving both textual and visual content from the original document. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate simple lexical or semantic matching, and most methods encode pages independently. Consequently, they overlook the contextual information in the document required to resolve queries that aggregate information across multiple pages. In this paper, we introduce CMDR and CMDR-Bench, a new multimodal document retrieval task and benchmark that require modeling document context. To address this challenge, we propose CMDR-Embed, a contextual multimodal embedding framework that explicitly incorporates document context by jointly encoding multiple pages and deriving page-level embeddings from a shared contextual representation. Furthermore, we introduce CMCL, a contextual multimodal contrastive learning objective that effectively trains CMDR-Embed by balancing contextual modeling with page-level discriminability. Experiments demonstrate that CMDR-Embed significantly outperforms non-contextual embeddings, highlighting the importance of context-aware multimodal embeddings for advancing document retrieval.

entry.title: InfluMatch: Frontier-Quality KOL Search at 4B-Model Cost [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matching influencers (KOLs) to free-form, multi-part Thai marketing criteria is today served either by keyword search over structured profiles, which misses semantic fit, or by prompting frontier LLMs over every candidate, which is accurate but slow and expensive. We present InfluMatch, a low-cost three-stage cascade -- retrieval $\rightarrow$ rerank $\rightarrow$ reason -- built entirely from small open-weight models: dense retrieval returns 50 candidates, a 4B pointwise reranker scores each by the log-probability of a single Yes token and keeps 10, and a 4B reasoner grades the shortlist per criterion on a rubric with a Thai rationale. The cascade is designed for cost: reasoning over a filtered top-10 halves token spend versus reasoning over all 50 while scoring 14 points higher. End-to-end against human relevance labels on an 11-query set with all 50 candidates labeled, the full cascade reaches 94.1% P@5, versus a retrieval-only baseline near random; it matches the frontier model Kimi-K2.6 (91.8%) while emitting ${\sim}35\times$ fewer output tokens and serving a 50-KOL query in ${\sim}20$ s on one A100. Notably, the only fine-tuning that pays off is pairwise: a SimPO-tuned reranker matches the frontier baseline's best-pick accuracy (78.0 EM), whereas fine-tuning the reasoner on pointwise per-criterion labels improves offline scores yet degrades end-to-end ranking -- an inversion we trace to the design of the absolute labeling task -- leaving the untuned base model as the strongest deployed reasoner. The result is a deployable, explainable KOL search system at a small fraction of frontier serving cost.

entry.title: PluraMath: Extending Mathematical Reasoning Evaluation Beyond High-Resource Languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.05992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical reasoning has become a central task for evaluating and tuning reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs), yet existing benchmarks remain heavily biased toward high-resource languages, with English and Chinese dominating both pre-training corpora and evaluation suites. The recently released PolyMath (Wang et al., 2025) dataset represents a significant step forward, yet its coverage is still limited to 18 only high-resource languages. To address this gap, we introduce PluraMath, an extension of PolyMath to 18 additional {underrepresented languages spanning 6 language families -- ranging from mid-resource to extreme low-resource settings. We constructed the dataset through a human-curated pipeline, where native speakers thoroughly validated pre-computed translations. Using PluraMath, we then benchmark 27 reasoning LLMs across four model scales -- small, mid-size, large, and closed-source ensembles -- probing the multilingual mathematical reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art models under diverse linguistic conditions. Our fine-grained analysis confirms a persistent gap in mathematical reasoning performance between high-resource and underrepresented languages, with stronger results largely associated with better instruction-following ability. We fully open-source our dataset, data acquisition pipeline, and evaluation framework, with the goal of lowering the barrier to multilingual benchmark development for underrepresented communities.

entry.title: From Blueprint to Reality: Modeling and Applying Putnam's Social Capital Theory with LLM-based Multi-agent Simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.06080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Putnam's Social Capital Theory is a foundational framework for collective action and community prosperity. However, traditional empirical methods face practical limits on control and replication. Meanwhile, LLM-based social simulations are typically behavior-driven and lack theory-aligned environments for modeling Putnam's core propositions. To address these gaps, we introduce SocaSim, an LLM-based multi-agent simulation framework to study Putnam's Social Capital Theory from theoretical blueprint to simulated reality. Specifically, we build an environment integrating social network evolution, trust dynamics, and norm propagation, where agents engage in repeated collective-action experiments, and then apply the three dimensions to analyze adaptation challenges in smart elderly care. Our simulations reproduce Putnam's macro-level patterns and exhibit strong human-agent alignment at the group level. Unlike traditional methods, SocaSim traces micro-level causal pathways of social network, trust, and norms via round-by-round simulations and counterfactual interventions, enabling process-level interpretability. Taken together, these capabilities establish a research paradigm that leverages LLM agents to bridge social science and computer science.

entry.title: x-Prediction Is All You Need:Training-Free Accelerated Generation via Endpoint Decodability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.06114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models generate high-quality samples, but their ODE samplers often need tens to hundreds of neural function evaluations (NFEs). This remains a practical challenge for released checkpoints, since many accelerators require additional design choices and training cost through retraining, distillation, or trajectory redesign. We investigate a different route based on $x$-prediction. During sampling, standard affine probability paths already expose $x_0$ information: an intermediate state and its path velocity determine a principled estimate of the clean sample. We formalize this property as \textbf{endpoint decodability} and show that the decoder is the minimum-MSE estimator $\mathbb{E}[x_0\mid x_t]$ under the usual $\ell_2$ objective. This yields \textbf{Truncated Jump Sampling} (TJS): stop the ODE at an early-exit time $t^*$ and return the decoded $x_0$. TJS requires no retraining, distillation, or architecture change. Across SDXL, SD3.5M, Z-Image-Turbo, and three class-conditional benchmarks, it reduces NFEs by 20--70\% with near-matched quality. The analysis also shows why endpoint prediction can work without straightening the trajectory, providing inference acceleration without trajectory redesign.

entry.title: Static Metrics Are Insufficient: Predicting Java Method Energy Usage with Execution Time
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.06124v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The increasing energy demand of software systems is raising concerns about their environmental impact and associated costs. Reasoning on energy usage early in the development flow has the potential to significantly reduce the overall energy usage of a software system, as it allows developers to make informed design and refactoring decisions before inefficiencies propagate. However, assessing energy usage without repeated profiling and direct measurement is difficult, which limits early reasoning in practice. This study investigates the limits of method-level energy prediction in Java, examining whether static source code metrics complemented with method-level execution time can estimate the energy consumption of Java methods. We profile 2,786 Java methods to extract 33 static features and measure execution time and energy, then train and compare eleven regression models. Our findings show that static source code metrics alone yield poor predictive performance, with average R2 values close to zero. Incorporating execution time as a lightweight dynamic input significantly improves accuracy, raising R2 to as high as 0.46. Execution time, internal method calls, and cyclomatic complexity consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of energy consumption.

entry.title: Self-Supervised Implicit CEST Reconstruction via Physics-Informed Lorentz Encoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.06132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Pool Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (CEST) MRI provides valuable metabolic information but is clinically limited by long acquisition times. Although sparse sampling reduces scanning time, reconstructing high-resolution Z-spectra from limited data remains an ill-posed inverse problem. Conventional interpolation and generic Implicit Neural Rep-resentations (INRs) often lack physical constraints, leading to spectral artifacts and physically invalid signals. To address this, we propose Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed framework that formulates CEST reconstruction as a self-supervised reconstruction task via implicit continuous coordinate learning. Unlike generic positional encodings, LE regularizes the continuous spectral mapping by projecting sparse coordinates into a physically constrained space governed by a combination of parametric Lorentzian profiles with learnable basis functions. This mechanism effectively reduces noise and enforces consistency with physical models. Experiments on in vivo human brain data demonstrate that LE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, under a 39-point sampling strategy, LE achieves a PSNR of 57.58 dB and an SSIM of 0.9994. Furthermore, the learned physics-informed encodings form a continuous, geometrically ordered trajectory in the latent space, ensuring accurate quantitative metabo-lite mapping (APT, NOE, MT).

entry.title: LLM Agents for Deliberative Collaboration: A Study on Joint Decision Making Under Partial Observability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.06157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deliberation plays a crucial role in collaboration; when humans work together, they naturally engage in communication to align information and reach an agreement. In this paper, we investigate deliberative large language model (LLM) agents under partially observable joint decision-making tasks. We formalize deliberative collaboration as a cooperative joint decision problem with partial and asymmetric observations, and introduce a scalable benchmark that instantiates this problem across multiple task settings and domains in which agents must exchange information through deliberation to reach a joint decision with a shared reward. We then instantiate a reference scaffold and evaluation protocol for deliberative agents and conduct a systematic evaluation of a range of representative LLMs. The results reveal that complex deliberative collaboration tasks continue to challenge state-of-the-art language models. Even with the aid of external mathematical tools, language models may fail in either the deliberation process for aligning information or the complex reasoning process for making the decision. On the other hand, diagnostic analysis reveals that the deliberation process may also provide opportunities for reflection and error correction, sometimes improving performance over centralized baselines. Altogether, our work establishes a foundation for evaluating and improving LLM agents in deliberative collaboration and provides insights into the strengths, limitations, and properties of current LLM-based multi-agent systems.

entry.title: LongCrafter: Towards Diverse Long-Context Understanding via Evidence-Graph-Guided Instruction Synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
